title: When the body fits but the sleeves do not: Alter, size up, or walk away?
summary: A top that fits through the torso can still restrict the upper arms. The right response depends on whether the pressure comes from the sleeve, armhole, shoulder, or lining—and whether the garment has enough structure and value to alter.
author: Curvy& Editorial

sections.heading: Tight sleeves are a proportion problem, not a wrong-body problem
paragraphs: In a recent r/PlusSizeFashion discussion, a shopper described a repeated mismatch: shirts fit the torso but squeeze larger upper arms. Community responses clustered around three strategies—buy for the arms and tailor the body, choose stretchier or roomier sleeve shapes, or add fabric with a gusset. Each can work, but only after identifying where the garment is actually restrictive.

A sleeve can be tight at the bicep while the armhole and shoulder fit correctly. It can also feel tight because the armhole is too low or narrow, the shoulder seam sits in the wrong place, the sleeve cap limits movement, or a lining is smaller than the outer layer. Pulling across the chest or back can travel into the sleeve as well.

sections.heading: Diagnose the pressure before changing the size
paragraphs: Measure the fullest part of your upper arm while relaxed, then measure the sleeve of a garment that fits. For a woven top, the finished sleeve needs wearing ease beyond the body measurement; Cashmerette notes that one to three inches is a common patternmaking range, although the right amount depends on fabric and intended silhouette. Stretch knits may use less ease or even negative ease, so circumference alone is not the whole answer.

During try-on, let your arms hang, reach forward as if driving, lift them overhead, and cross them in front of your chest. Note whether the pressure stays around the bicep or pulls the armhole, shoulder, back, or bust. If the cuff is the only tight point, that is a different and usually simpler alteration than rebuilding a set-in sleeve.

sections.heading: Sizing up works only while the shoulders still belong to you
paragraphs: Buying the size that clears the arms and taking in the torso is often the cleanest ready-to-wear solution. Side seams, waist seams, or back darts can remove excess body width. This route is most practical when the larger size still places the shoulder seam near the shoulder point and keeps the neckline, bust shaping, armhole, and overall length in useful positions.

The approach becomes expensive when sizing up moves every landmark. A tailor may then need to narrow shoulders, reset sleeves, reshape the armhole, move darts, and shorten the garment—not merely take in two side seams. For coats, blazers, and lined dresses, ask for an estimate before removing tags. Fit the hardest structural area first, but do not assume an arbitrarily larger size can always be rebuilt economically.

sections.heading: A gusset can rescue the right garment
paragraphs: A gusset is an inserted piece of fabric that adds width or movement at a stressed seam. Threads describes set-in sleeve gussets as a way to widen a snug bicep and improve range of motion; iFixit's repair guide demonstrates the method on an existing shirt. It is especially plausible when the torso and shoulder already fit, the underarm seam is accessible, and matching or intentionally contrasting fabric is available.

The alteration is less discreet on transparent fabric, an uninterrupted print, leather, heavy tailoring, or a garment with complex lining. Seam allowance, sleeve construction, and the amount of width needed determine whether a narrow wedge is enough or a larger insert must continue into the body. A professional tailor should inspect valuable or structured pieces before anything is cut.

sections.heading: Choose future sleeves by movement, not by a style name alone
paragraphs: Raglan, dolman, flutter, lantern, and intentionally full sleeves can provide more room than a close set-in sleeve, while stretch fabric can make small measurement differences more forgiving. None is an automatic guarantee. Seamwork notes that the sleeve and armhole are engineered together; cap height, armhole depth, bicep ease, and shoulder placement all affect movement.

When shopping online, ask for finished bicep circumference, armhole depth, sleeve opening, shoulder width, and fabric stretch. Compare them with a successful garment rather than relying on a model photograph or the word relaxed. If those measurements are unavailable and returns are costly, a sleeveless layer plus a well-fitting cardigan or jacket may be a lower-risk system than repeatedly buying woven sleeves blind.
bullets: Keep the garment if movement is comfortable and the sleeve leaves no deep pressure marks.
Size up and tailor when the larger shoulder and armhole still align well.
Consider a gusset when the problem is localized and suitable matching fabric exists.
Walk away when several structural areas are wrong or alteration cost exceeds the garment's value.

researchNote: This guide synthesizes a September 2026 community discussion and established sewing and repair guidance. Community suggestions are individual experiences; alteration feasibility depends on the garment, seam allowance, fabric, lining, and required change, so high-value pieces should be assessed by a tailor.
